misconception_description: Student believes that conditional statements, i.e., Python statements that evaluate to either True or False, must always be wrapped in if/else statements to be returned as Boolean values.

solutions.generated_code:
program MatriksIdentitas
kamus
  n, i, j : integer
  baris : string
  diagonal : boolean
algoritma
  input(n)
  for i <- 1 to n do
    baris <- ""
    for j <- 1 to n do
      if i == j then
        diagonal <- true
      else
        diagonal <- false
      endif
      if diagonal then
        baris <- baris + "1 "
      else
        baris <- baris + "0 "
      endif
    endfor
    output(baris)
  endfor
endprogram

metadata.modification_notes: The student rewrote the solution to use a helper function `is_diagonal(i, j)` that checks if position (i, j) is on the diagonal of the matrix. Due to their misconception, the student believes they must wrap the comparison `i == j` in an if/else statement to return a boolean value, rather than simply returning `i == j` directly. The code still functions correctly and produces the right identity matrix, but demonstrates the unnecessary verbosity that comes from this misconception. The student genuinely believes this is the proper way to return boolean values from conditional expressions.
